client: I've been really stressed about school since the start of the new semester. Ever since I got that B- on my final project last term, I can't stop worrying that I'll lose my scholarship if my grades slip again. I know I should be focusing on my current classes, but I keep replaying that last project in my head and second-guessing all my work now.
therapist: I hear how much that past grade is still weighing on you, and how it's making it hard to focus on the present. When you describe replaying that project in your head, I notice your voice sounds a bit withdrawn—like part of you might be feeling defeated before you even begin your new work. What do you think keeps pulling your mind back to that one grade?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I keep going back to that grade because it feels like proof I'm not as smart as everyone thinks I am. Even though it was last semester, I can't shake this fear that I'll mess up again and people will finally see I'm not good enough. 

It's stupid because logically I know one bad grade doesn't define me, but the anxiety just won't go away no matter how much I try to reason with myself.
therapist: That fear of being "found out" sounds really painful—like you're carrying this weight of expectation that one misstep will reveal some truth about you. I notice when you talk about this, your voice gets very quiet, almost like you're shrinking from the thought itself. What do you think would happen if you *did* let yourself believe that one grade truly doesn't define you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I know logically that one grade doesn't define me, but it *feels* like proof that I'm not as smart as people think. If I start believing it doesn't matter, then I worry I'll get complacent and stop trying so hard. That pressure to keep up appearances is exhausting, but it also feels necessary.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between wanting to ease this pressure and feeling like it's the only thing keeping you going—that must be exhausting to carry. I notice your voice speeds up when you talk about this, like the worry itself is chasing you. What would it look like to find a balance between pushing yourself and allowing yourself some compassion?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client:
It *is* exhausting, but I don't know how to stop. If I'm not constantly pushing myself, I feel like I'll fall behind or disappoint everyone. The idea of self-compassion sounds nice, but it just feels like an excuse to be lazy. 

I guess part of me knows this isn't sustainable, but the guilt kicks in whenever I try to slow down. Like last weekend when I tried to take a break, I ended up just lying there thinking about all the things I *should* be doing.
therapist: It sounds like even when you try to rest, your mind keeps pulling you back into that cycle of "shoulds"—like taking a break feels more like abandoning your responsibilities than actually recharging. That must leave you feeling stuck between needing rest and feeling guilty for it. What do you think it would take for a break to truly feel restorative rather than like something you "shouldn't" be doing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't even know what would make rest feel okay anymore. It's like there's always this voice in my head saying "you could be doing something productive right now" whenever I try to relax. Maybe if I finished all my work first... but the list never ends, so that's not really possible.
therapist: That voice sounds relentless—like no matter how much you do, it's never enough to "earn" rest. I notice your words and your tone both carry this heavy exhaustion, like you're running on empty but can't stop. What would it be like to experiment with short breaks where the goal isn't productivity, but just noticing how your body and mind feel in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
